summary: An experimental extension to NHRP that lets mobile Next Hop Clients register and attach to a Next Hop Server in their home Logical IP Subnet in an authenticated manner.

eli5.summary: When a traveling computer wants to tell its home network where it is now, this document gives a safe way to check it is really who it says it is.

questions: what is the mobile nhc authentication extension
how does end-to-end authentication differ from hop-by-hop authentication
how do mobile clients register with nhrp safely
subtitle: Safe registration of mobile computers with NHRP authentication

tldr.problem: Mobile NHRP clients cannot safely register with their home server through intermediate servers because NHRP's hop-by-hop authentication requires a trust relationship with every server on the path, which is impractical for mobile clients.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an end-to-end authentication extension that allows a mobile client to sign its NHRP registration request with a key it shares only with its home server. Intermediate servers ignore the extension and forward the request; only the home server verifies the signature.
tldr.outcome: Mobile clients can register securely without trusting intermediate servers, enabling nomadic use cases. The solution preserves hop-by-hop authentication for other security purposes and can be combined with it for defense-in-depth.

facts.label: Key management
facts.value: Manual configuration or Internet standard protocols

today: RFC 2520 is an Experimental extension to NHRP. ATM networks and NHRP itself have faded from active use, so this protocol remains undeployed but documents an important security pattern: end-to-end authentication for nomadic clients.

sections.title: Mobile Clients and NHRP Registration
sections.content:
NHRP (Next Hop Resolution Protocol) is used in ATM and NBMA (Non-Broadcast Multi-Access) networks to resolve layer 3 addresses to layer 2 (ATM) addresses, allowing hosts to communicate directly. A mobile NHC (Next Hop Client) is one that is not configured with the address of its home server but can discover one through other means, such as an anycast address. When a mobile client finds an NHS (Next Hop Server), it may be a surrogate (temporary) server, not the client's home server.

To establish a direct ATM connection, the mobile client must register with its home server, which is reached by routing the registration request through the network. The home server then sets up a virtual circuit to the client. However, NHRP's standard authentication is hop-by-hop: each intermediate server verifies the request before forwarding it. This requires the mobile client to share keys with every server on the path, which is impractical. This RFC introduces end-to-end authentication as an alternative.
sections.eli5: A traveling computer connects to a helper server to ask "where is my home server?" The helper forwards the question, but the traveling computer needs to prove who it is to its real home, not to the helper.

sections.title: End-to-End Authentication
sections.content:
Traditional hop-by-hop authentication requires the sender to share a key with every server that will process the packet. For a nomadic client, this is infeasible because the path and intermediate servers are unknown in advance. End-to-end authentication instead allows the client to compute a cryptographic signature over the entire request using a key shared only with the destination (the home server). Intermediate servers that do not understand the extension simply ignore it and forward the packet unchanged, following the principle that an NHS must ignore extensions it does not recognize.

The extension is anchored in the registration packet and covers the fixed part, mandatory NHRP header fields, and all extensions up to and including the Mobile NHC Authentication Extension. If hop-by-hop and end-to-end authentication are both present, both will be checked independently: intermediate servers validate hop-by-hop authentication, and the home server validates the end-to-end signature.
sections.eli5: Instead of proving your identity at each step, you write a secret message that proves who you are to the final destination. Helpers along the way do not need to check it.

sections.title: Authentication Extension Format
sections.content:
The Mobile NHC Authentication Extension includes four main fields: a Security Parameter Index (SPI), the source address from the outgoing interface, the source ATM address, and the authentication data (the computed signature). The SPI acts as a key index into a table maintained by the client and server, allowing them to select the correct cryptographic key and algorithm without transmitting the key itself.

The tuple of SPI and source address uniquely identifies which key was used. The signature is computed over the entire NHRP payload up to and including the authentication extension, with the authentication data field initially zeroed. The sending client allocates the SPI value and populates the associated table entry with the key, algorithm, and lifetime. HMAC-MD5-128 is the mandatory default algorithm, though others may be negotiated. Keys can be configured manually or negotiated using an Internet standard key management protocol.
sections.eli5: The secret message includes a number that says which secret key was used, so the home server knows which key to check with. It also includes the message itself and a signature to prove who sent it.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
End-to-end authentication protects against spoofing on the home subnet by verifying the signature with a key known only to the sender and the home server. The authentication covers the entire NHRP payload from the fixed header through the authentication extension itself, guaranteeing both source authenticity and data integrity. If the authentication check fails, the packet is simply dropped; no error indication is returned because the surrogate server cannot route a reply back to an unregistered mobile client.

The RFC recommends strong key selection, as the security of the entire system depends on it. Hop-by-hop and end-to-end authentication can be used together: hop-by-hop provides access control at the first point of contact, while end-to-end authentication provides protection against compromise of intermediate servers. If neither is used, the system is vulnerable to spoofing and active attacks. The RFC also notes that encryption must be provided by layer 3 mechanisms; the authentication extension provides only integrity and source authentication, not confidentiality.
sections.eli5: The signature proves who the message came from and that it was not changed along the way. If the signature is wrong, the message is thrown away. You can use both the signature method and the old hop-by-hop checks together for extra safety.
